19. Nonsmooth Convex Optimization

CNRS & DMA, École Normale Supérieure

Chapter PDF · Complete book

Many recovery and learning problems combine smooth losses with constraints or penalties that are not differentiable. Solving them efficiently requires understanding both the cost of an iteration and the conditions for convergence. We begin with subgradient, projection, and barrier methods, then develop proximal maps and splitting algorithms, including ADMM and primal–dual schemes.

The main references for this chapter are [10, 11, 4]. Further background is provided in [25, 3, 2].

We consider a general convex optimization problem

min⁡x∈H  f(x)(19.1)\underset{x \in \mathcal{H}}{\min}\; f(x) \tag{19.1}x∈Hmin​f(x)(19.1)

where H=Rp\mathcal{H}=\mathbb{R}^pH=Rp is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, and seek algorithms with a low cost per iteration. The first-order methods below use gradients, subgradients, or proximal maps. Unless stated otherwise, functions are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and a minimizer is assumed to exist.

19.1 Descent Methods¶

We extend the gradient method of Section 14.4 to nonsmooth objectives and constraints.

19.1.1 Gradient Descent¶

The optimization problem (9.26) is an unconstrained problem of the form (19.1) with a smooth objective: f:H→Rf : \mathcal{H}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}f:H→R is continuously differentiable with Lipschitz gradient. Here ∇f(x)∈H\nabla f(x)\in\mathcal{H}∇f(x)∈H is the gradient of the objective with respect to its variable xxx. It is distinct from the spatial gradient ∇x\nabla x∇x of a signal or image, which is a vector field. The functional gradient satisfies the first-order expansion

f(x+r)=f(x)+⟨∇f(x), r⟩H+O(∣ ⁣∣r∣ ⁣∣H2)f(x+r) = f(x) + \langle \nabla f(x),\,r\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} + O(|\!| r |\!|_{\mathcal{H}}^2)f(x+r)=f(x)+⟨∇f(x),r⟩H​+O(∣∣r∣∣H2​)

The Lipschitz-gradient assumption gives the quadratic remainder O(∣ ⁣∣r∣ ⁣∣H2)O(|\!| r |\!|_{\mathcal{H}}^2)O(∣∣r∣∣H2​); differentiability alone gives o(∣ ⁣∣r∣ ⁣∣H)o(|\!| r |\!|_{\mathcal{H}})o(∣∣r∣∣H​). Examples of gradient computations appear in Section 9.5.3.

For such a function, the gradient descent algorithm is defined as

x(ℓ+1):=x(ℓ)−τℓ∇f(x(ℓ)).(19.2)x^{(\ell+1)} \mathrel{:=}x^{(\ell)} - \tau_\ell \nabla f( x^{(\ell)} ). \tag{19.2}x(ℓ+1):=x(ℓ)−τℓ​∇f(x(ℓ)).(19.2)

The step size τℓ>0\tau_\ell>0τℓ​>0 balances stability against progress per iteration.

19.1.2 Subgradient Method¶

For a nonsmooth objective fff, replace the gradient in (19.2) by a subgradient:

x(ℓ+1):=x(ℓ)−τℓg(ℓ)whereg(ℓ)∈∂f(x(ℓ)).(19.3)x^{(\ell+1)} \mathrel{:=}x^{(\ell)} - \tau_\ell g^{(\ell)} \quad \text{where} \quad g^{(\ell)} \in \partial f( x^{(\ell)} ). \tag{19.3}x(ℓ+1):=x(ℓ)−τℓ​g(ℓ)whereg(ℓ)∈∂f(x(ℓ)).(19.3)

A subgradient step need not decrease the objective. Convergence generally requires diminishing step sizes, as the example f(x)=∣x∣f(x)=|x|f(x)=∣x∣ illustrates. This can make the method slow. When the objective admits a useful decomposition, the proximal methods developed below can exploit it more effectively.

Theorem 19.1

Assume fff is convex, a minimizer x⋆x^\starx⋆ exists, and the chosen subgradients satisfy ∣ ⁣∣gℓ∣ ⁣∣⩽G|\!| g^\ell |\!|\leqslant G∣∣gℓ∣∣⩽G. If ∑ℓτℓ=+∞\sum_\ell\tau_\ell=+\infty∑ℓ​τℓ​=+∞ and ∑ℓτℓ2<+∞\sum_\ell\tau_\ell^2<+\infty∑ℓ​τℓ2​<+∞, then the iterates converge to a minimizer. More generally,

min⁡0⩽ℓ<N{f(xℓ)−f(x⋆)}⩽∣ ⁣∣x0−x⋆∣ ⁣∣2+G2∑ℓ<Nτℓ22∑ℓ<Nτℓ.\min_{0\leqslant\ell<N}\{f(x^\ell)-f(x^\star)\} \leqslant\frac{|\!| x^0-x^\star |\!|^2+G^2\sum_{\ell<N}\tau_\ell^2}{2\sum_{\ell<N}\tau_\ell}.0⩽ℓ<Nmin​{f(xℓ)−f(x⋆)}⩽2∑ℓ<N​τℓ​∣∣x0−x⋆∣∣2+G2∑ℓ<N​τℓ2​​.

For a prescribed horizon NNN and positive bounds D,GD,GD,G, the constant step τℓ=D/(GN)\tau_\ell=D/(G\sqrt N)τℓ​=D/(GN​) gives a bound DG/NDG/\sqrt NDG/N​ when ∣ ⁣∣x0−x⋆∣ ⁣∣⩽D|\!| x^0-x^\star |\!|\leqslant D∣∣x0−x⋆∣∣⩽D. A step 1/(ℓ+1)1/(\ell+1)1/(ℓ+1) satisfies the convergence conditions but does not, by itself, give an O(N−1/2)O(N^{-1/2})O(N−1/2) bound.

19.1.3 Projected Gradient Descent¶

We consider a constrained optimization problem

min⁡x∈C  f(x)(19.4)\underset{x \in \mathcal{C}}{\min}\; f(x) \tag{19.4}x∈Cmin​f(x)(19.4)

where C⊂RS\mathcal{C}\subset \mathbb{R}^SC⊂RS is a nonempty closed convex set and f:RS→Rf : \mathbb{R}^S \rightarrow \mathbb{R}f:RS→R is convex and continuously differentiable. The convergence theorem below additionally assumes a Lipschitz gradient.

To impose the constraint, follow the gradient step (19.2) by projection:

x(ℓ+1):=ProjC(x(ℓ)−τℓ∇f(x(ℓ))).(19.5)x^{(\ell+1)} \mathrel{:=}\mathop{\mathrm{Proj}}_\mathcal{C}\left( x^{(\ell)} - \tau_\ell \nabla f( x^{(\ell)} ) \right). \tag{19.5}x(ℓ+1):=ProjC​(x(ℓ)−τℓ​∇f(x(ℓ))).(19.5)

Here ProjC\mathop{\mathrm{Proj}}_\mathcal{C}ProjC​ is the orthogonal projection onto C\mathcal{C}C, defined by

ProjC(x)=argminx′∈C  ∣ ⁣∣x−x′∣ ⁣∣\mathop{\mathrm{Proj}}_\mathcal{C}(x) = \underset{x' \in \mathcal{C}}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; |\!| x-x' |\!|ProjC​(x)=x′∈Cargmin​∣∣x−x′∣∣

The projection is unique because C\mathcal{C}C is nonempty, closed, and convex.

Projected gradient retains analogous convergence guarantees under the following assumptions.

Theorem 19.2

Assume fff is convex with LLL-Lipschitz gradient, C\mathcal{C}C is nonempty, closed, and convex, and a constrained minimizer exists. For a fixed 0<τ<2/L0<\tau<2/L0<τ<2/L, projected gradient descent converges to a constrained minimizer. If 0<τ⩽1/L0<\tau\leqslant 1/L0<τ⩽1/L, then for ℓ⩾1\ell\geqslant 1ℓ⩾1,

f(xℓ)−f(x⋆)⩽∣ ⁣∣x0−x⋆∣ ⁣∣22τℓ.f(x^\ell)-f(x^\star)\leqslant\frac{|\!| x^0-x^\star |\!|^2}{2\tau\ell}.f(xℓ)−f(x⋆)⩽2τℓ∣∣x0−x⋆∣∣2​.

If fff is μ\muμ-strongly convex, the iterates converge linearly.

Proof

This is the special case g=ιCg=\iota_\mathcal{C}g=ιC​ of Theorem 19.14. In the strongly convex case, the gradient step is a contraction for the admissible fixed step sizes, and composition with the nonexpansive projector preserves that property.

The main practical difficulty in (19.5) is evaluating the projection. For several sets arising in ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1 minimization, it can be computed efficiently.

19.2 Interior Point Methods¶

We briefly describe interior-point methods, which often require relatively few but expensive iterations. They extend Newton-type methods to problems whose constraints have a suitable barrier representation, such as nonnegativity of vectors or positive definiteness of matrices.

To illustrate the main idea, we consider the following problem

min⁡x∈Rd,Ax⩽y  f(x)(19.6)\underset{x\in \mathbb{R}^d, A x \leqslant y}{\min}\; f(x) \tag{19.6}x∈Rd,Ax⩽ymin​f(x)(19.6)

for A∈Rm×dA \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}A∈Rm×d.

Related formulations replace the vector AxA xAx by a matrix and the componentwise inequality ⩽\leqslant⩽ by a positive-semidefinite constraint.

Example 19.3 (Lasso)

The Lasso problem (applied to the regression problem Bw≈bBw \approx bBw≈b for B∈Rn×pB \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}B∈Rn×p)

with λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 can be recast as (19.6) by introducing nonnegative variables x=(x−,x+)∈R2px=(x_-,x_+) \in \mathbb{R}^{2p}x=(x−​,x+​)∈R2p (so that d=2pd=2pd=2p) and w=x+−x−w = x_+ - x_-w=x+​−x−​ with (x+,x−)⩾0(x_+,x_-) \geqslant 0(x+​,x−​)⩾0, so that f(x)=12∣ ⁣∣B(x+−x−)−b∣ ⁣∣2+λ⟨x, 1⟩f(x) = \frac{1}{2}|\!| B(x_+-x_-)-b |\!|^2 + \lambda\langle x,\,\mathbb{1}\ranglef(x)=21​∣∣B(x+​−x−​)−b∣∣2+λ⟨x,1⟩, A=−Id2pA=-\mathrm{Id}_{2p}A=−Id2p​, and y=0y=0y=0 (so that m=2pm=2pm=2p).

Example 19.4 (Dual of the Lasso)

Alternatively, solve the dual of (19.7):

min⁡∣ ⁣∣B⊤q∣ ⁣∣∞⩽1  f(q)=λ2∣ ⁣∣q∣ ⁣∣2−⟨q, b⟩(19.8)\underset{|\!| B^\top q |\!|_\infty \leqslant 1}{\min}\; f(q)=\frac{\lambda}{2}|\!| q |\!|^2-\langle q,\,b\rangle \tag{19.8}∣∣B⊤q∣∣∞​⩽1min​f(q)=2λ​∣∣q∣∣2−⟨q,b⟩(19.8)

so that one can use A=(B⊤−B⊤)A=\begin{pmatrix} B^\top \\-B^\top \end{pmatrix}A=(B⊤−B⊤​) and the constraint right-hand side is 12p\mathbb{1}_{2p}12p​ (so that d=nd=nd=n and m=2pm=2pm=2p).

Interior-point methods approximate (19.6) by introducing a logarithmic barrier:

min⁡x∈Rd, Ax<y  ft(x):=f(x)−1tLog(y−Ax)(19.9)\underset{x\in\mathbb{R}^d,\ Ax<y}{\min}\; f_t(x) \mathrel{:=}f(x) - \frac{1}{t} \text{Log}( y-A x ) \tag{19.9}x∈Rd, Ax<ymin​ft​(x):=f(x)−t1​Log(y−Ax)(19.9)

where

Log(u):=∑ilog⁡(ui)\text{Log}(u) \mathrel{:=}\sum_i \log(u_i)Log(u):=i∑​log(ui​)

The function −Log-\mathrm{Log}−Log is strictly convex and diverges at the boundary of the positive orthant.

Assuming strict feasibility and existence of central-path minimizers x(t)x(t)x(t), the objective values f(x(t))f(x(t))f(x(t)) approach the original optimal value as t→+∞t\to+\inftyt→+∞.

For a fixed ttt, assume ftf_tft​ is twice continuously differentiable with positive definite Hessian along the iterates. Apply Newton’s method to (19.9), using a line search such as Armijo backtracking (14.14) to choose 0<τℓ⩽10<\tau_\ell\leqslant 10<τℓ​⩽1 while maintaining Ax(ℓ)<yAx^{(\ell)}<yAx(ℓ)<y:

x(ℓ+1):=x(ℓ)−τℓ[∂2ft(x(ℓ))]−1∇ft(x(ℓ))(19.10)x^{(\ell+1)} \mathrel{:=}x^{(\ell)} - \tau_\ell [ \partial^2 f_t(x^{(\ell)})]^{-1} \nabla f_t(x^{(\ell)}) \tag{19.10}x(ℓ+1):=x(ℓ)−τℓ​[∂2ft​(x(ℓ))]−1∇ft​(x(ℓ))(19.10)

The gradient and Hessian are

∇ft(x)=∇f(x)+1tA⊤1y−Axand∂2ft(x)=∂2f(x)+1tA⊤diag(1(y−Ax)2)A.\nabla f_t(x) = \nabla f(x) + \frac{1}{t} A^\top \frac{1}{y-Ax} \quad \text{and} \quad \partial^2 f_t(x) = \partial^2 f(x) + \frac{1}{t} A^\top \mathop{\mathrm{diag}}\left( \frac{1}{(y-Ax)^2} \right) A.∇ft​(x)=∇f(x)+t1​A⊤y−Ax1​and∂2ft​(x)=∂2f(x)+t1​A⊤diag((y−Ax)21​)A.

A natural stopping criterion for the inner Newton iterations is

⟨[∂2ft(x(ℓ))]−1∇ft(x(ℓ)), ∇ft(x(ℓ))⟩<ε2.\langle [ \partial^2 f_t(x^{(\ell)})]^{-1} \nabla f_t(x^{(\ell)}),\,\nabla f_t(x^{(\ell)})\rangle < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}.⟨[∂2ft​(x(ℓ))]−1∇ft​(x(ℓ)),∇ft​(x(ℓ))⟩<2ε​.

The barrier method approximately minimizes ftf_tft​ through (19.10), tracing the central path t↦x(t)t \mapsto x(t)t↦x(t) for increasing parameters t=tk=μkt0t=t_k=\mu^k t_0t=tk​=μkt0​ with μ>1\mu > 1μ>1.

A warm start makes this continuation strategy efficient: initialize the Newton iterations (19.10) for x(tk)x(t_k)x(tk​) at the preceding solution x(tk−1)x(t_{k-1})x(tk−1​).

Along the central path, the logarithmic barrier gives f(x(tk))−f(x⋆)⩽m/tkf(x(t_k))-f(x^\star) \leqslant m/t_kf(x(tk​))−f(x⋆)⩽m/tk​, where mmm is the number of scalar constraints. To reach error ε\varepsilonε, take k=0,…,Kk=0, \ldots, Kk=0,…,K with

mtK=mt0μK⩽ε.\frac{m}{t_{K}} = \frac{m}{t_0 \mu^{K}} \leqslant\varepsilon.tK​m​=t0​μKm​⩽ε.

Thus O(∣log⁡(ε)∣)O(|\log(\varepsilon)|)O(∣log(ε)∣) barrier-parameter updates suffice for accuracy ε\varepsilonε. The total cost also depends on the number of inner Newton iterations (19.10), whose control requires further assumptions on fff.

The relevant complexity theory uses self-concordant barriers. A convex function φ\varphiφ on a line is self-concordant when

∣φ(3)(s)∣⩽2φ′′(s)3/2.|\varphi^{(3)}(s)|\leqslant 2\varphi''(s)^{3/2}.∣φ(3)(s)∣⩽2φ′′(s)3/2.

The logarithmic barrier has this property. For a linear objective, the appropriately scaled objective tf−Log(y−Ax)t f-\mathrm{Log}(y-Ax)tf−Log(y−Ax) is self-concordant; arbitrary positive rescaling does not preserve the same self-concordance constant. With a suitable path-following neighborhood and barrier-parameter schedule, the number of Newton steps can be bounded polynomially in the problem parameters and logarithmically in 1/ε1/\varepsilon1/ε. The bound depends on the barrier parameter (equal to mmm for this logarithmic barrier), not only on the requested accuracy. A fixed number of Newton steps per outer iteration cannot be asserted for an arbitrary update factor μ>1\mu>1μ>1.

19.3 Proximal Algorithm¶

For a nonsmooth objective fff, an explicit gradient step may be undefined. An implicit step remains available even when fff is nonsmooth.

19.3.1 Proximal Map¶

For a step size τ>0\tau>0τ>0, define the proximal map by

∀ x,Proxτf(x):=argminx′  12∣ ⁣∣x−x′∣ ⁣∣2+τf(x′).(19.11)\forall \,x, \quad \mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau f}(x) \mathrel{:=}\underset{x'}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; \frac{1}{2}|\!| x-x' |\!|^2+\tau f(x'). \tag{19.11}∀x,Proxτf​(x):=x′argmin​21​∣∣x−x′∣∣2+τf(x′).(19.11)

It balances a decrease in fff against a quadratic penalty for moving away from xxx.

Since f∈Γ0(H)f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal{H})f∈Γ0​(H), the objective 12∣ ⁣∣x−⋅∣ ⁣∣2+τf\frac12|\!| x-\cdot |\!|^2+\tau f21​∣∣x−⋅∣∣2+τf is strongly convex and coercive, so Proxτf\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau f}Proxτf​ is well defined and single-valued.

For an indicator f=ιCf=\iota_\mathcal{C}f=ιC​, the proximal map is the projection ProxιC=ProjC\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\iota_\mathcal{C}}=\mathop{\mathrm{Proj}}_{\mathcal{C}}ProxιC​​=ProjC​. It therefore generalizes projection to convex functions. For each fixed input, the proximal point is also the projection onto a suitable sublevel set of fff. Like an orthogonal projection, the proximal map is nonexpansive.

Proposition 19.5

One has ∣ ⁣∣proxf(x)−proxf(y)∣ ⁣∣⩽∣ ⁣∣x−y∣ ⁣∣|\!| \mathop{\mathrm{prox}}_{f}(x)-\mathop{\mathrm{prox}}_{f}(y) |\!| \leqslant|\!| x-y |\!|∣∣proxf​(x)−proxf​(y)∣∣⩽∣∣x−y∣∣.

The following identities simplify proximal computations.

Proxf+⟨y, ⋅⟩=Proxf(⋅−y),Proxf(⋅−y)=y+Proxf(⋅−y).\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{f+\langle y,\,\cdot\rangle}=\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_f(\cdot-y), \quad \mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{f(\cdot-y)} = y + \mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{f}(\cdot-y).Proxf+⟨y,⋅⟩​=Proxf​(⋅−y),Proxf(⋅−y)​=y+Proxf​(⋅−y).

If f(x)=∑k=1Kfk(xk)f(x)=\sum_{k=1}^K f_k(x_k)f(x)=∑k=1K​fk​(xk​) for x=(x1,…,xK)x=(x_1,\ldots,x_K)x=(x1​,…,xK​) is separable, then

Proxτf(x)=(Proxτfk(xk))k=1K.(19.14)\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau f}(x) = ( \mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau f_k}(x_k) )_{k=1}^K. \tag{19.14}Proxτf​(x)=(Proxτfk​​(xk​))k=1K​.(19.14)
Proof

The optimality condition for z=Proxf+⟨y, ⋅⟩(x)z=\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{f+\langle y,\,\cdot\rangle}(x)z=Proxf+⟨y,⋅⟩​(x) is 0∈z−x+∂f(z)+y0\in z-x+\partial f(z)+y0∈z−x+∂f(z)+y, or x−y∈z+∂f(z)x-y\in z+\partial f(z)x−y∈z+∂f(z). Thus z=Proxf(x−y)z=\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_f(x-y)z=Proxf​(x−y). For the translated function, substitute w=z−yw=z-yw=z−y in min⁡z{12∣ ⁣∣z−x∣ ⁣∣2+f(z−y)}\min_z\{\frac12|\!| z-x |\!|^2+f(z-y)\}minz​{21​∣∣z−x∣∣2+f(z−y)} to obtain z=y+Proxf(x−y)z=y+\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_f(x-y)z=y+Proxf​(x−y). Separability follows by minimizing each coordinate block independently.

Composition with a linear map having orthonormal rows admits an explicit formula.

Proposition 19.8

If A∈RP×NA \in \mathbb{R}^{P \times N}A∈RP×N satisfies AA∗=IdPAA^*=\mathrm{Id}_PAA∗=IdP​, then

Proxf∘A=A∗∘Proxf∘A+IdN−A∗A.\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{f \circ A} = A^* \circ \mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{f} \circ A + \mathrm{Id}_N - A^* A.Proxf∘A​=A∗∘Proxf​∘A+IdN​−A∗A.

In particular, if AAA is orthogonal, then Proxf∘A=A∗∘Proxf∘A\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{f \circ A} = A^* \circ \mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{f} \circ AProxf∘A​=A∗∘Proxf​∘A.

19.3.3 Related Concepts¶

Link with the subdifferential.

For a set-valued map U:H↪GU : \mathcal{H}\hookrightarrow \mathcal{G}U:H↪G, we define the inverse set-valued map U−1:G↪HU^{-1} : \mathcal{G}\hookrightarrow \mathcal{H}U−1:G↪H by

h∈U−1(g)⟺g∈U(h)(19.15)h \in U^{-1}(g) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g \in U(h) \tag{19.15}h∈U−1(g)⟺g∈U(h)(19.15)

The proximal map is the resolvent of the subdifferential.

Proposition 19.9

One has Proxτf=(Id+τ∂f)−1\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau f} = (\mathrm{Id}+\tau\partial f)^{-1}Proxτf​=(Id+τ∂f)−1.

Proof

The optimality condition gives the equivalences

z=Proxτf(x)⇔0∈z−x+τ∂f(z)⇔x∈(Id+τ∂f)(z)⇔z=(Id+τ∂f)−1(x)z = \mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau f}(x) \Leftrightarrow 0 \in z-x+\tau\partial f(z) \Leftrightarrow x \in (\mathrm{Id}+\tau\partial f)(z) \Leftrightarrow z = (\mathrm{Id}+\tau\partial f)^{-1}(x)z=Proxτf​(x)⇔0∈z−x+τ∂f(z)⇔x∈(Id+τ∂f)(z)⇔z=(Id+τ∂f)−1(x)

The final relation is an equality because the inverse is single-valued here.

This resolvent interpretation connects proximal algorithms with the theory of maximally monotone operators.

Link with duality.

Moreau decomposition relates the proximal maps of a function and its conjugate.

Theorem 19.10 (Moreau decomposition)

One has

Proxτf=Id−τProxf∗/τ(⋅/τ).\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau f} = \mathrm{Id}- \tau \mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{f^* / \tau}( \cdot/\tau ).Proxτf​=Id−τProxf∗/τ​(⋅/τ).

Thus a tractable proximal map for fff gives one for f∗f^*f∗, and conversely.

For example, Proposition 18.7 gives the following expression for soft thresholding

Proxτ∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣1(x)=x−τProj∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣∞⩽1(x/τ)=x−Proj∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣∞⩽τ(x)whereProj∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣∞⩽τ(x)=min⁡(max⁡(x,−τ),τ).\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau |\!| \cdot |\!|_1}(x) = x - \tau \mathop{\mathrm{Proj}}_{|\!| \cdot |\!|_\infty \leqslant 1}( x/\tau ) = x - \mathop{\mathrm{Proj}}_{|\!| \cdot |\!|_\infty \leqslant\tau}( x ) \quad \text{where} \quad \mathop{\mathrm{Proj}}_{|\!| \cdot |\!|_\infty \leqslant\tau}( x ) = \min(\max(x,-\tau),\tau).Proxτ∣∣⋅∣∣1​​(x)=x−τProj∣∣⋅∣∣∞​⩽1​(x/τ)=x−Proj∣∣⋅∣∣∞​⩽τ​(x)whereProj∣∣⋅∣∣∞​⩽τ​(x)=min(max(x,−τ),τ).

The minimum and maximum in this clipping formula act componentwise.

For an indicator f=ιCf=\iota_{\mathcal{C}}f=ιC​ of a closed convex cone C\mathcal{C}C,

(ιC)∗=ιC∘whereC∘:={y  ;  ∀ x∈C,⟨x, y⟩⩽0}(19.16)(\iota_{\mathcal{C}})^* = \iota_{\mathcal{C}^\circ} \quad \text{where} \quad \mathcal{C}^\circ \mathrel{:=} \left\{ y \;;\; \forall \,x \in \mathcal{C}, \langle x,\,y\rangle \leqslant 0 \right\} \tag{19.16}(ιC​)∗=ιC∘​whereC∘:={y;∀x∈C,⟨x,y⟩⩽0}(19.16)

where C∘\mathcal{C}^\circC∘ is the polar cone. This conjugacy relation (19.16) is specific to cones: for a general convex set C\mathcal{C}C, the conjugate of its indicator need not be an indicator.

Equation (19.16) yields Moreau polar decomposition:

x=ProjC(x)+⊥ProjC∘(x)x = \mathop{\mathrm{Proj}}_{\mathcal{C}}(x) +^\bot \mathop{\mathrm{Proj}}_{\mathcal{C}^\circ}(x)x=ProjC​(x)+⊥ProjC∘​(x)

The notation +⊥+^\bot+⊥ indicates that the two summands are orthogonal.

For a linear subspace C=V\mathcal{C}=VC=V, this reduces to the orthogonal decomposition Rp=V⊕⊥V⊥\mathbb{R}^p = V \oplus^\bot V^\botRp=V⊕⊥V⊥.

A proximal step is also a gradient step on the Moreau–Yosida envelope fμf_\mufμ​ of fff from (18.4).

One has

Proxμf=Id−μ∇fμ.\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\mu f} = \mathrm{Id}- \mu \nabla f_\mu.Proxμf​=Id−μ∇fμ​.

19.4 Proximal Gradient Algorithms¶

Splitting algorithms exploit a decomposition of the objective into terms whose proximal maps can be computed separately.

Different decompositions of the same objective produce different splitting algorithms. A useful decomposition balances the cost of the proximal maps against the convergence of the resulting iteration.

Step sizes and other parameters also need to be chosen; theoretical convergence bounds and line-search strategies can guide their selection.

19.4.1 Proximal Point Algorithm¶

One has the following equivalence

x⋆∈argminf⇔0∈∂f(x⋆)⇔x⋆∈(Id+τ∂f)(x⋆)(19.17)\begin{aligned} x^\star \in \mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}f &\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad 0 \in \partial f(x^\star) \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x^\star \in (\mathrm{Id}+\tau \partial f)(x^\star) \end{aligned} \tag{19.17}x⋆∈argminf​⇔0∈∂f(x⋆)⇔x⋆∈(Id+τ∂f)(x⋆)​(19.17)
⇔x⋆=(Id+τ∂f)−1(x⋆)=Proxτf(x⋆).(19.18)\begin{aligned} &\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x^\star = (\mathrm{Id}+\tau \partial f)^{-1}(x^\star) = \mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau f}(x^\star). \end{aligned} \tag{19.18}​⇔x⋆=(Id+τ∂f)−1(x⋆)=Proxτf​(x⋆).​(19.18)

This shows that being a minimizer of fff is equivalent to being a fixed point of Proxτf\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau f}Proxτf​.

This fixed-point characterization suggests the proximal point iterations

x(ℓ+1):=Proxτℓf(x(ℓ)).(19.19)x^{(\ell+1)} \mathrel{:=}\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau_\ell f}(x^{(\ell)}). \tag{19.19}x(ℓ+1):=Proxτℓ​f​(x(ℓ)).(19.19)

The proximal point method does not require an upper stability bound on the step size. Steps must nevertheless be large enough in aggregate; the following sufficient condition is convenient.

Theorem 19.12

If 0<τmin⁡⩽τℓ⩽τmax⁡<+∞0<\tau_{\min} \leqslant\tau_\ell \leqslant\tau_{\max} < +\infty0<τmin​⩽τℓ​⩽τmax​<+∞, then x(ℓ)→x⋆x^{(\ell)} \rightarrow x^\starx(ℓ)→x⋆ for a minimizer of fff.

This implicit step (19.19) should be compared with a gradient descent step (19.2)

x(ℓ+1):=(Id−τℓ∇f)(x(ℓ)).x^{(\ell+1)} \mathrel{:=}(\mathrm{Id}-\tau_\ell\nabla f)(x^{(\ell)}).x(ℓ+1):=(Id−τℓ​∇f)(x(ℓ)).

The implicit resolvent (Id+τℓ∂f)−1(\mathrm{Id}+\tau_\ell\partial f)^{-1}(Id+τℓ​∂f)−1 replaces the explicit map Id−τℓ∇f\mathrm{Id}-\tau_\ell\nabla fId−τℓ​∇f. For small τℓ\tau_\ellτℓ​ and smooth fff, the two agree to first order. The implicit step also remains well defined for nonsmooth objectives and converges under the assumptions above, without the upper step-size restriction of explicit gradient descent. This resembles the greater stability of implicit Euler integration. The computational tradeoff is that a general proximal map may be as difficult to evaluate as the original minimization problem.

19.4.2 Forward–Backward Splitting¶

For a general objective, evaluating Proxγf\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\gamma f}Proxγf​ may be as difficult as solving the original problem.

A tractable alternative exploits a decomposition into a smooth term and a term with an accessible proximal map:

min⁡x  E(x):=f(x)+g(x)(19.20)\underset{x}{\min}\; \mathcal{E}(x) \mathrel{:=}f(x) + g(x) \tag{19.20}xmin​E(x):=f(x)+g(x)(19.20)

where g∈Γ0(H)g \in \Gamma_0(\mathcal{H})g∈Γ0​(H) can be nonsmooth, whereas fff is convex and has a Lipschitz gradient.

For this structure, the fixed-point argument (19.17) becomes

x⋆∈argminf+g⇔0∈∇f(x⋆)+∂g(x⋆)⇔x⋆−τ∇f(x⋆)∈(Id+τ∂g)(x⋆)⇔x⋆=(Id+τ∂g)−1∘(Id−τ∇f)(x⋆).\begin{aligned} x^\star \in \mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}f + g & \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad 0 \in \nabla f(x^\star) + \partial g(x^\star) \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x^\star - \tau \nabla f(x^\star) \in (\mathrm{Id}+\tau \partial g)(x^\star) \\ & \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x^\star = ( \mathrm{Id}+ \tau \partial g )^{-1} \circ ( \mathrm{Id}- \tau \nabla f ) (x^\star). \end{aligned}x⋆∈argminf+g​⇔0∈∇f(x⋆)+∂g(x⋆)⇔x⋆−τ∇f(x⋆)∈(Id+τ∂g)(x⋆)⇔x⋆=(Id+τ∂g)−1∘(Id−τ∇f)(x⋆).​

This fixed point suggests the following algorithm, known as forward–backward splitting

x(ℓ+1):=Proxτℓg(x(ℓ)−τℓ∇f(x(ℓ))).(19.21)x^{(\ell+1)} \mathrel{:=}\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau_\ell g}\left( x^{(\ell)} - \tau_\ell \nabla f(x^{(\ell)}) \right). \tag{19.21}x(ℓ+1):=Proxτℓ​g​(x(ℓ)−τℓ​∇f(x(ℓ))).(19.21)

Derivation using surrogate functionals.

A quadratic surrogate gives another derivation of the algorithm and helps explain its convergence.

Replace the objective E(x)\mathcal{E}(x)E(x) at the current iterate by a surrogate E(x,x(ℓ))\mathcal{E}(x,x^{(\ell)})E(x,x(ℓ)) that is easier to minimize, and define

x(ℓ+1):=argminx  E(x,x(ℓ)).(19.22)x^{(\ell+1)} \mathrel{:=}\underset{x}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; \mathcal{E}(x,x^{(\ell)}). \tag{19.22}x(ℓ+1):=xargmin​E(x,x(ℓ)).(19.22)

Require the surrogate to majorize the objective and agree with it at the current point:

E(x)⩽E(x,x′)andE(x,x)=E(x)(19.23)\mathcal{E}(x) \leqslant\mathcal{E}(x,x') \quad \text{and} \quad \mathcal{E}(x,x) = \mathcal{E}(x) \tag{19.23}E(x)⩽E(x,x′)andE(x,x)=E(x)(19.23)

and E(x)−E(x,x′)\mathcal{E}(x)-\mathcal{E}(x,x')E(x)−E(x,x′) should be a smooth function.

Property (19.23) ensures that E\mathcal{E}E does not increase along the iterations:

E(x(ℓ+1))⩽E(x(ℓ))\mathcal{E}(x^{(\ell+1)}) \leqslant\mathcal{E}(x^{(\ell)})E(x(ℓ+1))⩽E(x(ℓ))

For proximal-gradient surrogates with a fixed 0<τ<1/L0<\tau<1/L0<τ<1/L, sufficient decrease and the optimality conditions imply that every accumulation point is a minimizer. The majorization and touching conditions alone do not establish this conclusion for arbitrary surrogate schemes.

To construct a surrogate for (19.20), use the quadratic upper bound (14.19) supplied by the LLL-Lipschitz gradient of fff:

f(x)⩽f(x′)+⟨∇f(x′), x−x′⟩+L2∣ ⁣∣x−x′∣ ⁣∣2,f(x) \leqslant f(x') + \langle \nabla f(x'),\,x-x'\rangle + \frac{L}{2}|\!| x-x' |\!|^2,f(x)⩽f(x′)+⟨∇f(x′),x−x′⟩+2L​∣∣x−x′∣∣2,

so that for 0<τ<1L0 < \tau < \frac{1}{L}0<τ<L1​, the function

E(x,x′):=f(x′)+⟨∇f(x′), x−x′⟩+12τ∣ ⁣∣x−x′∣ ⁣∣2+g(x)(19.24)\mathcal{E}(x,x') \mathrel{:=}f(x') + \langle \nabla f(x'),\,x-x'\rangle + \frac{1}{2\tau}|\!| x-x' |\!|^2 + g(x) \tag{19.24}E(x,x′):=f(x′)+⟨∇f(x′),x−x′⟩+2τ1​∣∣x−x′∣∣2+g(x)(19.24)

satisfies the surrogate conditions (19.23).

Minimizing this surrogate is exactly a proximal-gradient step.

Proposition 19.13

The update (19.22) for the surrogate (19.24) is exactly (19.21).

Proof

This follows from the fact that

⟨∇f(x′), x−x′⟩+12τ∣ ⁣∣x−x′∣ ⁣∣2=12τ∣ ⁣∣x−(x′−τ∇f(x′))∣ ⁣∣2+cst.\langle \nabla f(x'),\,x-x'\rangle + \frac{1}{2\tau}|\!| x-x' |\!|^2 = \frac{1}{2\tau} |\!| x - (x'-\tau \nabla f(x')) |\!|^2 + \text{cst}.⟨∇f(x′),x−x′⟩+2τ1​∣∣x−x′∣∣2=2τ1​∣∣x−(x′−τ∇f(x′))∣∣2+cst.

**Convergence of FB. **

The majorization argument uses τ⩽1/L\tau\leqslant 1/Lτ⩽1/L, whereas convergence of the iterates holds on the larger interval 0<τ<2/L0<\tau<2/L0<τ<2/L.

Theorem 19.14

Let fff be convex with LLL-Lipschitz gradient and g∈Γ0(H)g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal{H})g∈Γ0​(H), and assume argmin(f+g)≠∅\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}(f+g)\neq\emptysetargmin(f+g)=∅. For a fixed step 0<τ<2/L0<\tau<2/L0<τ<2/L, the forward–backward iterates converge to a minimizer. If 0<τ⩽1/L0<\tau\leqslant 1/L0<τ⩽1/L, then

(f+g)(xℓ)−min⁡(f+g)⩽∣ ⁣∣x0−x⋆∣ ⁣∣22τℓ,ℓ⩾1.(f+g)(x^\ell)-\min(f+g)\leqslant\frac{|\!| x^0-x^\star |\!|^2}{2\tau\ell},\qquad\ell\geqslant 1.(f+g)(xℓ)−min(f+g)⩽2τℓ∣∣x0−x⋆∣∣2​,ℓ⩾1.

If fff is μ\muμ-strongly convex, the iterates converge linearly. In particular, for 0<τ⩽1/L0<\tau\leqslant 1/L0<τ⩽1/L, ∣ ⁣∣xℓ+1−x⋆∣ ⁣∣⩽(1−τμ)∣ ⁣∣xℓ−x⋆∣ ⁣∣|\!| x^{\ell+1}-x^\star |\!|\leqslant(1-\tau\mu)|\!| x^\ell-x^\star |\!|∣∣xℓ+1−x⋆∣∣⩽(1−τμ)∣∣xℓ−x⋆∣∣.

Taking g=ιCg=\iota_{\mathcal{C}}g=ιC​ in (19.21) recovers projected gradient descent (19.5), because the proximal map of an indicator is the projection onto the constraint set.

Applying (19.21) efficiently requires a tractable proximal map Proxτg\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau g}Proxτg​. A closed form is available for several useful penalties, including the ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1 penalty used by ISTA in Section 10.3.3.

19.5 Primal-Dual Algorithms¶

Convex duality, developed in Section 18.3, suggests new algorithms and allows existing methods to be applied to dual formulations.

19.5.1 Forward–Backward Splitting on the Dual¶

As a first example, apply a familiar method to the Fenchel–Rockafellar problem (18.12):

p⋆=inf⁡x  f(x)+g(Ax),(19.25)p^\star = \underset{x}{\inf}\; f(x) + g(A x), \tag{19.25}p⋆=xinf​f(x)+g(Ax),(19.25)

Assume additionally that fff is μ\muμ-strongly convex, and, for simplicity, that fff and ggg are finite and continuous everywhere. Even if fff is smooth, applying forward–backward splitting directly to the primal problem requires Proxτ(g∘A)\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau(g\circ A)}Proxτ(g∘A)​. This map can be difficult to evaluate despite having a simple Proxτg\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau g}Proxτg​. Proposition 19.8 gives an explicit formula in the special case AA∗=IdAA^*=\mathrm{Id}AA∗=Id.

Example 19.15 (TV denoising)

min⁡x  12∣ ⁣∣y−x∣ ⁣∣2+λ∣ ⁣∣∇x∣ ⁣∣1,2(19.26)\underset{x}{\min}\; \frac{1}{2}|\!| y-x |\!|^2 + \lambda|\!| \nabla x |\!|_{1,2} \tag{19.26}xmin​21​∣∣y−x∣∣2+λ∣∣∇x∣∣1,2​(19.26)

∣ ⁣∣v∣ ⁣∣1,2:=∑i∣ ⁣∣vi∣ ⁣∣.|\!| v |\!|_{1,2} \mathrel{:=}\sum_i |\!| v_i |\!|.∣∣v∣∣1,2​:=i∑​∣∣vi​∣∣.

Here

f=12∣ ⁣∣⋅−y∣ ⁣∣2andg=λ∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣1,2f=\frac{1}{2}|\!| \cdot-y |\!|^2 \quad \text{and} \quad g=\lambda|\!| \cdot |\!|_{1,2}f=21​∣∣⋅−y∣∣2andg=λ∣∣⋅∣∣1,2​

Example 19.16 (Support Vector Machine)

We consider a supervised classification problem with data (ai∈Rp,yi∈{−1,+1})i=1n(a_i \in \mathbb{R}^p, y_i \in \{-1,+1\})_{i=1}^n(ai​∈Rp,yi​∈{−1,+1})i=1n​.

min⁡x∈Rp  ∑iℓ(−yi⟨x, ai⟩)+λ2∣ ⁣∣x∣ ⁣∣2=λ2∣ ⁣∣x∣ ⁣∣2+g(Ax)(19.27)\underset{x\in\mathbb{R}^p}{\min}\;\sum_i\ell(-y_i\langle x,\,a_i\rangle) + \frac{\lambda}{2}|\!| x |\!|^2 = \frac{\lambda}{2}|\!| x |\!|^2 + g(A x) \tag{19.27}x∈Rpmin​i∑​ℓ(−yi​⟨x,ai​⟩)+2λ​∣∣x∣∣2=2λ​∣∣x∣∣2+g(Ax)(19.27)

p⋆=sup⁡u  −g∗(u)−f∗(−A∗u).(19.28)p^\star = \underset{u}{\sup}\; - g^*(u) - f^*(-A^*u). \tag{19.28}p⋆=usup​−g∗(u)−f∗(−A∗u).(19.28)

using differentiability of f∗f^*f∗.

In the particular case of the TV denoising problem (19.26), one has

g∗=ι∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣∞,2⩽λwhere∣ ⁣∣v∣ ⁣∣∞,2:=max⁡i  ∣ ⁣∣vi∣ ⁣∣g^* = \iota_{|\!| \cdot |\!|_{\infty,2} \leqslant\lambda} \quad \text{where} \quad |\!| v |\!|_{\infty,2} \mathrel{:=}\underset{i}{\max}\;|\!| v_i |\!|g∗=ι∣∣⋅∣∣∞,2​⩽λ​where∣∣v∣∣∞,2​:=imax​∣∣vi​∣∣

Remark 19.21 (Inverting structured linear operators)

Projection computations often require the inverse of a matrix of the form AA∗AA^*AA∗, A∗AA^*AA∗A, IdP+AA∗\mathrm{Id}_P+AA^*IdP​+AA∗ or IdN+A∗A\mathrm{Id}_N+A^*AIdN​+A∗A (see for instance (19.31)). The structure of the operator can make this inexpensive. For inpainting, AA∗AA^*AA∗ is diagonal. For deconvolution or partial Fourier measurements such as MRI, A∗AA^*AA∗A is diagonalized by the Fourier transform.

When inversion is expensive, primal-dual methods can replace it by applications of AAA and A∗A^*A∗, trading cheaper iterations for a potentially larger iteration count.

The alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) is related to Douglas–Rachford splitting on the dual problem (19.28). This formulation uses Proxτg∗\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau g^*}Proxτg∗​, computable from Proxτg\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau g}Proxτg​ by Moreau decomposition, and Proxτ(f∗∘A∗)\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau(f^*\circ A^*)}Proxτ(f∗∘A∗)​. 19.5.4 Primal-Dual Splitting¶

If neither Proxτg∘A\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau g \circ A}Proxτg∘A​ nor Proxτf⋆∘A∗\mathop{\mathrm{Prox}}_{\tau f^\star\circ A^*}Proxτf⋆∘A∗​ is tractable, a primal-dual method can work directly with the saddle problem. Its efficiency depends on the available operator evaluations, proximal maps, and conditioning.

For the structured problem (19.25), biconjugacy g=(g∗)∗g=(g^*)^*g=(g∗)∗ gives the saddle formulation

inf⁡x  f(x)+g(Ax)=inf⁡x  f(x)+sup⁡u  ⟨Ax, u⟩−g∗(u)=sup⁡u  inf⁡x  f(x)+⟨Ax, u⟩−g∗(u).(19.36)\begin{aligned} \underset{x}{\inf}\; f(x) + g(Ax) = \underset{x}{\inf}\; f(x) + \underset{u}{\sup}\; \langle Ax,\,u\rangle - g^*(u) = \underset{u}{\sup}\; \underset{x}{\inf}\; f(x) + \langle Ax,\,u\rangle - g^*(u). \end{aligned} \tag{19.36}xinf​f(x)+g(Ax)=xinf​f(x)+usup​⟨Ax,u⟩−g∗(u)=usup​xinf​f(x)+⟨Ax,u⟩−g∗(u).​(19.36)

We assume a primal-dual saddle point exists, so strong duality holds; strong convexity of fff is not required.
